turn_text: You're listening to the spoken edition of The Philadelphia Citizen. Within about a half-hour of one another, two revealing and ultimately hope-inducing press releases hit my inbox earlier this week. The first conveyed the news that Congressman Brendan Boyle had received something called the Newsweek Stubble Field Civility Award. Apparently the Stubblefield Institute for Civil Political Discourse partners with Newsweek to highlight lawmakers who, quote, bridge partisan divides and foster respectful debate. Boyle is a natural fit for the accolade. I've known him for something like 15 years, and I can't think of a more naturally civil person. Decorum, it turns out, does matter. And when norms are shattered like this... It's not about him, it's not about me. I'd be a winner, not really. It not only sours the political process, it makes an already disengaged electorate even more cynical. This gets us to the second press release heralding Republican Brian Fitzpatrick, who according to the Luger Center, was Congress's most bipartisan legislator. This reminder in rapid fire succession that rumors of the death of civility and bipartisanship may yet be premature was just what I needed, so I reached out to boil myself. What follows is some of the most important points of our in-depth conversation this week. I actually want to thank you, Boyle said, for having an interest in this and wanting to write about it, because I know just as well as you do that my winning an award on civility will not get nearly as many clicks or likes as if I went on Twitter and screamed my head off about something. The truth is, real bipartisanship still does exist, and it's necessary if you're going to get important pieces of legislation passed. So, if you'll remember, the Women and Lung Cancer Bill is my bill, and I invited Brian Fitzpatrick to be my Republican co-lead on it. I won't get really into the weeds on this, but basically, non-smoker women are contracting lung cancer at an alarming rate, and nobody knows why. The way I was able to get Republicans to act on this wasn't just my relationship with Brian, but also the lead Republican on the subcommittee, Brett Guthrie. He and I had become friends over the years. Here was an example where having that preexisting friendship really made a difference, where I was able to go to him and say, listen, this is not partisan and I could really use your help on this. Larry asked if relationships are so key to getting stuff done, why do I keep hearing that the members of opposite parties don't socialize like they used to? Boyle responded, obviously I didn't serve in the 70s and the 80s, but it's true that there's a lot less socializing together. The positive of living in your district is you are more connected to the folks who voted for you. But there is a downside, there's less time getting to know colleagues on the other side of the aisle. And let's face it, both political parties are now ideologically pure and consistent. Generations ago, you had two heterodox political parties. You had conservative Democrats, and you had liberal Democrats. You had conservative Republicans, and you had liberal Republicans. That made it easier to achieve bipartisan compromise. Nowadays, you have a totally right-wing Republican Party and a completely left-of-center Democratic Party. That makes it more difficult to actually achieve bipartisan compromise. But it is still possible. Larry asked for an example where Boyle exhibited civility with someone he might disagree with. In the budget committee boil said, the chair is Republican Jody Arrington, a conservative from West Texas. He and I have become very good friends. In hearings, I really tried to make it clear that our disagreements are about policy, not personality. I mean, there's no question that there's language police on the left who will react to you. That said, though, I do think it pales in comparison to what Donald Trump is doing on the right. I mean, people know that I'm close to President Biden. I've been a strong supporter of the administration, but there could be areas where I speak up and disagree. And unlike on the right, I'm not going to have to worry about either the president or any other Democrat trying to weigh in in primary me or sway people to vote against me. Whereas on the rides, boy, you step out of line just once and you have to worry about Donald Trump turning his fire on you. And then there's that whole media ecosystem they've built up on Twitter and on podcasts. I mean, they have a whole system in place to enforce discipline and to go after perceived heretics. That really doesn't exist on the left, certainly not to the same degree. Then Larry asked if, in the wake of the election, Boyle felt his party was going through the proper journey of introspection. Well, Boyle said, this touches on something that I care a lot about and I've been trying to work on for a number of years. The Democratic Party does have a working class voter problem. I found it, along with a colleague of mine, the blue-collar caucus eight years ago, to attempt to begin to address this disconnect. I genuinely believe that the policies and the economic programs of the Democratic Party are best for working-class Americans, and I genuinely believe that the Republican Party's economic program is heavily geared toward benefiting the top 1%. But I also have to recognize that a lot of working class voters did not reach the same conclusion in this past election. That trend really worries me. Larry asked if this was more a messaging problem. I do believe, Boyle said, we have a cultural disconnect between the way the Democratic Party is and the way it is perceived. Larry brought up the irony of Donald Trump, who inherited $400 million, being seen as some kind of Harry Truman champion of the working man. Yes, Boyle said, the anti-elitist with Elon Musk tagging along. It is genuinely sickening to me the way they've been able to cosplay as working class heroes. Larry then asked if Boyle could give an example where he'd stood up to an interest group of his party, or give an example where he's changed his mind on a substantive issue, kind of a test for political courage. The toughest vote I've cast in my career came in my first term, Boyle said. I came to the conclusion as a freshman member that the Iran nuclear deal was not worth doing, and that it was a mistake to lift sanctions on Iran and that brutal regime in Tehran. I do feel good about the vote. I think history, frankly, has proven my position to be correct, but boy, it was enormously difficult. I mean, I was heavily lobbied by the Obama White House. There were those who threatened me with a primary, not President Obama himself, not people close to him, but there were others. I was protested at one of my offices. That was a challenging time, and I was certainly going against the grain. Among House Democrats, I was one of 24 while the other 200 or so were voting for it. Well, thank you, Congressman Larry said, for taking the time and for your civility. Always fun talking to you, Boyle, politely replied. Thank you for listening. This has been a production of Citizencast.
